[Tabbu_ai]AI isn't running on code alone. It's running on copper, energy, and resources most people never think about. Everyone talks about AI models. Few talk about the metals needed to power them.
The real AI bottleneck may not be chips. It might be the raw materials behind them.
This puts the scale of the electrification challenge into perspective.
AI, EVs, data centers, renewables all roads seem to lead back to copper.
The future isn't just a software problem. It's a resource problem too. Here's the Stanford lecture rewritten in that storytelling style:
A Stanford professor just asked one of the most important questions of our generation.
What happens when AI can do everything humans can do...
But cheaper?
For decades, we've seen technologies reshape the world.
Electricity transformed industries.
Semiconductors powered the digital revolution.
The Internet connected billions of people.
Each created massive economic growth and changed how society works.
But AI may be different.
Why?
Because previous technologies automated tools.
AI automates intelligence itself.
And that's a much bigger shift.
Imagine a future where: ✅ AI handles research, writing, coding, analysis, and decision-making ✅ Robots handle manufacturing, logistics, construction, and physical labor ✅ Machines perform nearly every task humans can perform
Only faster. Only cheaper. Only at a scale no human workforce could match.
Sounds like science fiction.
But it's becoming a serious economic question.
And that's exactly what Stanford Professor Charles "Chad" Jones explores.
The discussion isn't about better chatbots.
Or faster computers.
It's about what happens when human labor is no longer the bottleneck.
What happens to jobs? What happens to wages? What happens to economic growth?
And perhaps the biggest question of all...
If machines can create most of the world's value, where does that leave humans?
Most people are debating AI prompts.
A few are thinking about how AI could reshape the entire economy.
The difference between those two conversations is enormous.
This lecture is worth watching.
Because the future may arrive much faster than most people expect. 👇 Full lecture below.

[ThiccTeddy]A complete breakdown of my top performing day trading strategy over the last 5 years:
It revolves around the 9ema
I use this strategy on the 5-minute chart. It also works on the 10 & 15, but I prefer the 5. I look for this setup during the morning trade window (30 minutes after open until noon)
This strategy works the best when the market is trending. Start by finding a day with a nice trend. Breakouts should have strong volume, pullbacks should have weak volume, key levels should be getting flipped
After you've isolated a strong trend, wait for a weak pullback to the 9ema. The volume should be low & the candles within the pullback should be small or medium sized. High volume on the pullback invalidates the setup. Large candles on the pullback invalidates the setup
You have 2 different entry points with this strategy:
1) Enter as the 9ema is tested. This is the lowest risk entry opportunity. Place your stop loss below the 9ema (with some wiggle room)
2) Enter after the 9ema forms a bounce. This has a higher win rate, but also more risk due to the wider gap between entry & stop loss
This simple strategy has paid me for years

[sudeepsriv]Anthropic built an AI so powerful, they couldn’t release the full version.
Instead, they split it in two.
Meet Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5.
Here’s the interesting part:
They are not two different models.
They’re essentially the same foundation model.
Claude Fable 5 is the version the public gets access to.
Claude Mythos 5 is the more capable version that remains heavily restricted because of its advanced capabilities, especially around cybersecurity and autonomous tasks.
Think of it like this:
Fable is the consumer release.
Mythos is what’s happening behind the curtain.
Why Anthropic did this:
As AI becomes more powerful, labs face a new problem.
How do you release cutting-edge intelligence without creating massive risks?
Anthropic’s answer was: • Release the safer version publicly • Keep the more capable version restricted • Gradually unlock capabilities as safeguards improve
This is becoming a trend across the industry.
We’re no longer asking:
“Can we build more powerful AI?"
We’re asking:
“How much of that power should be released?"
The real takeaway:
The gap between public AI models and frontier internal models is probably much larger than most people realize.
And Claude Mythos 5 might be one of the clearest examples of that.
My take:
The most interesting AI products today aren’t the ones being released.
They’re the ones companies aren’t comfortable releasing yet.

[dair_ai]Who should design the training environment for an RL agent, the practitioner or the policy itself?
RL pipelines for LLMs usually rely on manually redesigned environments between stages, with practitioners guessing which configuration will best improve the current policy.
This work proposes an LLM-as-Environment-Engineer framework. The current policy analyzes its own failure trajectories plus context and proposes the next-stage environment configuration, automating a step that has stayed stubbornly manual. They also release MAPF-FrozenLake, a controllable multi-agent testbed whose generator exposes multi-dimensional environment configs.
Why does it matter?
Curriculum design between RL stages is mostly gut feel today. Letting the policy read its failures and shape the next environment closes a loop that practitioners currently close by hand.
Paper: https://t.co/lZHlqozrQD

The consensus seems to be that leadership at Google has all but conceded that race to Anthropic and OpenAI, and that "only a big shake-up" will propel them back to the highs of mid-to-late 2025.
But employees are not hopeful: "We no longer have a frontier model in text, image, video, voice, or even vision... if we can't release a real frontier model after over four months of work with all of these resources, what are we doing?"
